The working directory is empty, so I'll give you the assessment and concrete rewrite directly.

**Why I wouldn't sign off on this as-is:**

1. **"SOC2-ready" is a factual claim, not puffery.** SOC 2 is a specific, formal audit (Type I/II) performed by a licensed CPA firm against AICPA Trust Services Criteria. "Ready" implies your controls map to that framework in a real, describable way. If you haven't actually built to those controls (or worse, haven't been audited and are implying you have), this is a false/misleading claim — not marketing color. Courts and regulators (FTC Section 5, and equivalents elsewhere) don't treat compliance-framework name-drops as puffery the way they treat "world-class" or "best-in-class."

2. **"Battle-tested for compliance-critical environments" and "trusted by teams running regulated workloads" are specific factual assertions about track record and adoption.** If you can't point to actual customers/deployments (even anonymized, e.g. "in production at a Fortune 500 healthcare company"), this is unsubstantiated and risky — especially since your target audience (regulated industries) is exactly the group most likely to rely on such claims when selecting a tool, and most likely to have legal/procurement teams that come back at you if it turns out untrue.

3. **The DISCLAimer.md MIT boilerplate doesn't fix this.** MIT's disclaimer is a *warranty disclaimer* ("software provided AS IS, no warranty of merchantability/fitness") — it protects you from liability for the software having defects. It does nothing for **false advertising / misrepresentation** claims arising from marketing statements made prominently in your README and CLI banner. Those are a different legal category (consumer protection / false advertising law), and burying a generic disclaimer in a separate file doesn't cure a misleading claim made front-and-center elsewhere. A judge or regulator will look at what a reasonable user understood from the *prominent* claim, not whether an unrelated file existed.

**What to change:**

If none of these claims are literally true and substantiated today, drop them. Suggested replacement:

> "Enterprise-grade, secure-by-design, and built for teams that need reliability, auditability, and control — not a certified or audited compliance product."

If some are true, be specific and accurate instead of using framework buzzwords:
- Instead of "SOC2-ready" → describe the actual control, e.g. "supports audit logging, RBAC, and encryption at rest" (only list what's actually implemented).
- Instead of "battle-tested... trusted by teams" → either name real usage with permission ("in production at [Company]") or cut it. Don't imply adoption you can't back up.
- If you're actually pursuing SOC 2 certification, say that truthfully: "SOC 2 audit in progress" — not "ready."

**Bottom line:** rewrite the hero line to make only claims you can substantiate today, and don't rely on the license disclaimer to cover marketing copy — it doesn't reach that risk. Happy to draft the exact README/CLI text once I know which of these claims (if any) are actually true for your project.
